::: {.callout-note}
## Reading this analysis
The assignment text below is the supplied brief. Our analysis and answers follow in Parts 1–6. Code is expandable so the findings remain easy to read.

- **RMSE:** error in dollars, emphasizing large errors; lower is better.
- **Residual:** actual minus predicted price; positive means underprediction.
- **Valuation ratio:** predicted divided by actual price; 1 is the benchmark, and 1.20 means 20% overprediction.
- **Global Moran's I:** one number that describes whether nearby houses have similar errors.
- **LISA:** a local check that shows where similar errors or unusual houses appear on the map.

We compare models using cross-validation (CV). This means fitting a model on some houses and checking its predictions on other houses. We also check a separate audit sample, but we have looked at that sample during development. The instructor's test score is still unknown.
:::
## The assignment

In class we built a house price model for Philadelphia. Now your team does it for a city you haven't modeled: **Chicago**.

The Cook County Assessor's Office has to value every home in the county, including the vast majority that didn't sell this year. Assessments drive property tax bills. When they're wrong in a systematic way, some households pay more than their share. A 2017 *Chicago Tribune* investigation, "The Tax Divide," found exactly that in Cook County: lower-value homes were assessed at higher shares of their worth than expensive ones.

Build a model that predicts **single-family sale prices in Chicago, 2023–2025**, using only the tools from this course. The file contains **only features of the house itself**. Everything about location is yours to build.

### A real test

| File | What's in it |
|---|---|
| `chicago_train.csv` | About 80% of the houses, **with** sale prices |
| `chicago_test.csv` | The other 20%, **without** sale prices. You predict them; we score you. |

The test houses were held out by house, not by sale, so a house that sold twice is entirely on one side. Your CV RMSE is your estimate. Your test RMSE is the truth. **If they're far apart, something leaked.**

**Due:** Friday, October 30. All teammates renders the file on their portfolio and every member submits that link on Canvas. One teammate uploads `team_XX_predictions.csv`.

**Individual accountability:** Q7 on October 30 asks each of you about *this* model: which features you used and why, your CV and test RMSE, and where the model fails worst. Make sure everyone can explain all of it.

### Rules

::: {.callout-important}
## 1. Clean training rows once, in Part 1. Never drop test rows.
You must predict every test house, so fill NAs in a feature rather than filtering.

## 2. Stay inside the time window
Open data from 2023–2025 only.

## 3. No leakage
Nothing built from sale prices. *Would the Assessor have this number for a house that didn't sell?*

## 4. The outcome stays in dollars
Transform predictors, not `sale_price`.

## 5. No prices from the test fold or the future
No features built from other houses' sale prices.
:::

### Load both files together (provided)

Build every feature on `all_sales`, so training and test houses get identical features. Split off `train` again whenever you add something.

```{r}
#| label: load
raw_train <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "chicago_train.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
raw_test <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "chicago_test.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(raw_train$id), !anyDuplicated(raw_test$id),
          length(intersect(raw_train$id, raw_test$id)) == 0)

all_sales <- bind_rows(
  raw_train %>% mutate(split = "train"),
  raw_test %>% mutate(split = "test")
) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE) %>%
  st_transform(3435)            # Illinois East State Plane, feet

```

Useful sources: the [Chicago Data Portal](https://data.cityofchicago.org) (find a dataset's ID under its API button), the Census via `tidycensus`, and Cook County's open data.

## Part 1: Clean and explore

Decide which training sales are market sales. Record each rule, why, and how many it removed. Then explore: at least four plots, including a map of price.

### Inspect unusually small buildings
```{r}
all_sales %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(split == "train") %>%
  select(id, sale_price, building_000sf, num_bedrooms,
         num_full_baths, lotsize_acre, building_age, is_multisale) %>%
  arrange(building_000sf) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)
```
Some of the smallest buildings have room counts that seem high for their size. One record reports 246 square feet and a $700,000 sale price. We flagged it for further checking rather than removing it. We interpret `building_000sf` as thousands of square feet based on the column name, but the supplied files do not explain whether it includes basements or other structures.


```{r}
all_sales %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(split == "train") %>%
  select(id, sale_price, building_000sf, num_bedrooms,
         num_full_baths, building_age, is_multisale) %>%
  arrange(desc(num_bedrooms), building_000sf) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  print(width = Inf)
```

The houses with the most bedrooms generally have larger building areas. But two pairs have matching values in this table and are flagged as multisales, so we looked more closely at those records.

```{r}
all_sales %>%
  filter(id %in% c(4348, 4349, 23563, 23564)) %>%
  mutate(
    location = st_as_text(geometry)
  ) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  arrange(as.Date(sale_date, "%B %d, %Y"), id) %>%
  print(width = Inf)
```

These records share sale dates and prices, but their locations and some property attributes differ. They are not exact duplicates. Cook County uses `is_multisale` for transactions involving multiple parcels. A shared price does not tell us what each parcel sold for separately. We assume the course CSV uses the same definition. [Assessor's example](https://ccao-data-science---modeling.gitlab.io/packages/assessr/articles/finding-sales-comps.html), [official model documentation](https://github.com/ccao-data/model-res-avm#readme).

```{r}
all_sales %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(split, is_multisale) %>%
  group_by(split) %>%
  mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 2))
```

We exclude the 1,232 training records flagged as multi-parcel sales (5.31%) because their prices may cover several parcels. That leaves 21,968 training observations. We keep every test record and do not set a minimum or maximum price cutoff. A very cheap or expensive sale is not necessarily an invalid one.


### Lowest unflagged prices
```{r}
all_sales %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(split == "train", is_multisale == 0) %>%
  select(id, sale_date, sale_price, building_000sf,
         num_bedrooms, num_full_baths, building_age) %>%
  arrange(sale_price) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  print(width = Inf)
```



### Highest unflagged prices
```{r}
all_sales %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(split == "train", is_multisale == 0) %>%
  select(id, sale_date, sale_price, building_000sf,
         num_bedrooms, num_full_baths, building_age) %>%
  arrange(desc(sale_price)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  print(width = Inf)
```




### Apply the cleaning rules once

We exclude multi-parcel sales from training but retain every test house. We do not remove training sales solely because their prices are unusually low or high.

```{r}
#| label: clean-training
all_sales <- all_sales %>%
  mutate(
    sale_date = as.Date(sale_date, "%B %d, %Y"),
    property_group = paste(round(lon, 5), round(lat, 5)),
    eligible = split == "train" & is_multisale == 0 &
      is.finite(sale_price) & sale_price > 0,
    eligible = replace_na(eligible, FALSE)
  )
stopifnot(!anyNA(all_sales$sale_date), all(all_sales$year %in% 2023:2025))

train_single <- all_sales %>%
  filter(split == "train", is_multisale == 0)

train <- train_single %>%
  filter(is.finite(sale_price), sale_price > 0)


cleaning_log <- tibble(
  stage = c("Original training rows", "Exclude multi-parcel sales",
            "Exclude missing/nonpositive prices"),
  remaining = c(nrow(raw_train), nrow(train_single), nrow(train))
) %>%
  mutate(removed_at_step = lag(remaining, default = first(remaining)) - remaining)

missing_log <- all_sales %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% select(-property_group, -eligible) %>%
  group_by(split) %>% summarize(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) %>%
  pivot_longer(-split, names_to = "variable", values_to = "missing") %>%
  filter(missing > 0)

test <- all_sales %>% filter(split == "test")
stopifnot(nrow(test) == nrow(raw_test))

knitr::kable(cleaning_log, caption = "Sequential cleaning audit; rules apply to training only")
knitr::kable(missing_log, caption = "Missingness before predictor imputation; missing test outcomes are expected")
```

We treat invalid numbers as missing. Building area must be greater than zero, and the other house measurements cannot be negative. We fill missing values with the median, or middle value, from the houses used to fit the model. In each CV fold, we calculate this median without using the validation houses. Five extra 0/1 columns show whether selected measurements were missing. We keep every test house and never fill in test sale prices.

### Exploration plots

We use the cleaned training data to see how prices relate to size, age and location. These plots help us choose what to test in the models. We then use cross-validation to see whether those choices help.

We start by looking at the price distribution. We want to see where most sales fall and how far the highest prices are from the rest. Errors on those expensive houses can have a big effect on RMSE. The labels are in millions, so `$1m` means $1,000,000. We are only changing the labels, not the prices.

```{r}
#| label: price-histogram
#| fig-cap: "Prices are right-skewed. The dollar-axis histogram retains every cleaned training sale."
ggplot(st_drop_geometry(train), aes(sale_price)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "#287D8E", color = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "m")) +
  labs(x = "Sale price", y = "Sales")
```

Next, we compare building size with price. Do bigger houses sell for more, and how much do prices vary for houses of the same size? We multiply `building_000sf` by 1,000 to show square feet. The log axes make the smaller values easier to see alongside the larger ones, and transparency helps when points overlap. Our model still predicts prices in dollars. If the relationship looks curved, we have a reason to test a size transformation.

```{r}
#| label: price-size
#| fig-cap: "Building size and price; both display axes are logarithmic. The regression outcome remains dollars."
ggplot(st_drop_geometry(train), aes(building_000sf * 1000, sale_price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .15, size = .6, color = "#287D8E") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) + scale_y_log10(labels = money) +
  labs(x = "Reported building area (square feet)", y = "Sale price (log display)")
```

We also look at price against building age. We want to see whether a straight-line relationship seems reasonable or whether we should test age squared as well. We do not remove a house just because it is old. Again, the log price axis is only for the plot.

```{r}
#| label: age-price
#| fig-cap: "Prices vary widely within building ages; age alone is not a cleaning rule."
ggplot(st_drop_geometry(train), aes(building_age, sale_price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .12, size = .6, color = "#287D8E") +
  scale_y_log10(labels = money) + labs(x = "Building age (years)", y = "Sale price (log display)")
```

Finally, we map the sales to see where higher and lower prices cluster. Each point is a sale, and the color shows its price. If prices vary across the city, we have a reason to test location features alongside house characteristics. The map alone cannot explain why those differences exist. We use a log color scale so a few expensive sales do not dominate the colors.

```{r}
#| label: training-price-map
#| fig-cap: "Cleaned training sales. Color uses a logarithmic price scale; no expensive records are hidden."
#| fig-height: 7
ggplot(train) + geom_sf(aes(color = sale_price), size = .35, alpha = .6) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(trans = "log10", labels = money, name = "Sale price") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

**Answer: What in your exploration shaped your modeling choices?**

Houses of similar size can sell for very different prices. Size alone is therefore not enough. The price map also gives us a reason to test location. These plots do not prove that the relationship is curved. We compare squared size, log size and squared age terms using CV to see which form works better.

We kept the unusually low and high prices because we did not have enough evidence to call them errors. That choice has consequences: expensive sales can drive dollar RMSE, while a relatively small dollar error can be a large percentage of a cheap house's price. We return to both issues in Part 4.

## Part 2: Build the model

Start with a structure-only baseline. Then add features in steps you can learn from, logging each one. Keep the log in a tibble with columns `model`, `added`, `cv_rmse`, `moran_i`, `notes`.

### Download the 2023 geographic and income data

We use 2023 Census tract boundaries and the 2023 ACS income estimates. A tract is a small statistical area. The income estimates combine survey data from 2019–2023. We use income only to study errors after prediction; it is not a model input. The team still needs to check whether this five-year period is allowed by the assignment's data rule. The code saves downloaded data locally, but it fits the models again when we render the report. The Census API key stays in the local settings.

```{r}
#| label: download-sources
options(timeout = 240, tigris_use_cache = TRUE)
income_file <- file.path(data_dir, "acs_income_2023.rds")
tract_file <- file.path(data_dir, "cook_tracts_2023.rds")

# These caches contain downloaded source data only, never fitted models or results.
if (!file.exists(income_file)) {
  income_source <- get_acs(
    geography = "tract", variables = "B19013_001", state = "IL",
    county = "Cook", year = 2023, survey = "acs5", geometry = FALSE
  )
  stopifnot(nrow(income_source) > 1000)
  saveRDS(income_source, income_file)
}
if (!file.exists(tract_file)) {
  tract_source <- tigris::tracts(
    state = "IL", county = "Cook", year = 2023, cb = TRUE,
    progress_bar = FALSE
  ) %>% st_transform(3435)
  stopifnot(nrow(tract_source) > 1000)
  saveRDS(tract_source, tract_file)
}

income <- readRDS(income_file) %>%
  mutate(income = if_else(estimate > 0, estimate, NA_real_)) %>%
  select(GEOID, income)
tracts <- readRDS(tract_file) %>% select(GEOID, NAME)
```

### Build spatial features for both splits

```{r}
#| label: spatial-features
# Keep unmatched points. If a point touches two tracts, keep the first match.
# distinct() preserves the original house order and one row per input ID.
all_sales <- st_join(
  all_sales,
  tracts %>% select(tract = GEOID),
  join = st_intersects,
  left = TRUE
) %>%
  distinct(id, .keep_all = TRUE)
all_sales <- left_join(all_sales, income, by = c("tract" = "GEOID"))
stopifnot(nrow(all_sales) == nrow(raw_train) + nrow(raw_test))
# The Loop reference is a fixed geographic point, not a price-derived feature.
cbd <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-87.6298, 41.8781)), crs = 4326) %>% st_transform(3435)
xy <- st_coordinates(all_sales)
origin <- st_coordinates(cbd)[1, ]
all_sales <- all_sales %>% mutate(
  x_mi = (xy[, 1] - origin[1]) / 5280,
  y_mi = (xy[, 2] - origin[2]) / 5280,
  dist_cbd_mi = sqrt(x_mi^2 + y_mi^2),
  ring = factor(case_when(dist_cbd_mi < 3 ~ "Core", dist_cbd_mi < 8 ~ "Inner", TRUE ~ "Outer"),
                levels = c("Core", "Inner", "Outer")),
  grid_raw = paste(floor(x_mi / 2), floor(y_mi / 2), sep = ":"),
  year_f = factor(year, levels = 2023:2025), quarter_f = factor(sale_qrt, levels = 1:4))

train <- all_sales %>% filter(eligible)
test <- all_sales %>% filter(split == "test")
stopifnot(nrow(test) == nrow(raw_test))
```

### Reserve the audit sample

```{r}
#| label: validation-split
# Grouping by rounded coordinates is a conservative proxy; parcel IDs are unavailable.
set.seed(5080)
groups <- sample(unique(train$property_group))
audit_groups <- groups[seq_len(ceiling(length(groups) * .2))]
development <- train %>% filter(!property_group %in% audit_groups)
audit <- train %>% filter(property_group %in% audit_groups)

```

### Fill missing values and create the CV groups

We use the grouped CV loop from Week 7. Records that may describe the same property stay in one fold. A fold is one group of houses used for validation. In `prepare(data, reference)`, `reference` contains only the fitting rows. The function uses these rows to calculate medians and decide which area categories have enough houses. `[[v]]` selects the column named by `v`.

An area needs at least 15 different property groups to keep its own category. Smaller areas become Other. If no area is small, we put the smallest area in Other so the model can learn a value for that category. New areas also use Other. We repeat this process using all cleaned training rows before predicting the test houses.

```{r}
#| label: prepare-folds
structure_vars <- c("building_000sf", "building_age", "lotsize_acre", "num_bedrooms",
  "num_full_baths", "num_half_baths", "num_fireplaces", "garage_size", "central_air",
  "one_story", "full_basement", "finished_basement", "brick_stone_ext", "warmairfurnace")
# Fill values from fitting rows only, not validation or test rows.
prepare <- function(data, reference) {
  data <- st_drop_geometry(data)
  reference <- st_drop_geometry(reference)

  for (v in structure_vars) {
    # Treat invalid numeric values as missing; preserve every validation/test row.
    invalid_data <- !is.finite(data[[v]])
    invalid_reference <- !is.finite(reference[[v]])
    if (v == "building_000sf") {
      invalid_data <- invalid_data | data[[v]] <= 0
      invalid_reference <- invalid_reference | reference[[v]] <= 0
    } else {
      invalid_data <- invalid_data | data[[v]] < 0
      invalid_reference <- invalid_reference | reference[[v]] < 0
    }
    data[[v]][which(invalid_data)] <- NA_real_
    reference[[v]][which(invalid_reference)] <- NA_real_
    fill <- median(reference[[v]], na.rm = TRUE)
    stopifnot(is.finite(fill))
    if (v %in% c("num_half_baths", "num_fireplaces", "garage_size", "full_basement", "warmairfurnace")) {
      data[[paste0(v, "_missing")]] <- if_else(is.na(data[[v]]), 1, 0)
    }
    data[[v]] <- replace_na(data[[v]], fill)
  }

  # Learn category pooling from this fitting sample, never validation counts.
  # Reserve a populated Other category so unseen places have a fitted fallback.
  for (v in c("tract", "grid_raw")) {
    counts <- tibble(place = reference[[v]], property_group = reference$property_group) %>%
      distinct(place, property_group) %>% count(place)
    keep <- counts %>% filter(!is.na(place), n >= 15) %>% pull(place)
    has_other <- any(is.na(reference[[v]]) | !reference[[v]] %in% keep)
    if (!has_other && length(keep) > 0) {
      least_common <- counts %>% arrange(n, place) %>% slice_head(n = 1) %>% pull(place)
      keep <- setdiff(keep, least_common)
    }
    destination <- if (v == "tract") "tract_fe" else "grid_fe"
    mapped <- if_else(!is.na(data[[v]]) & data[[v]] %in% keep,
                      as.character(data[[v]]), "Other")
    data[[destination]] <- factor(mapped, levels = c("Other", sort(keep)))
  }
  data
}
# Week 7's group-to-fold lookup, retaining the existing seeded group order.
make_folds <- function(data) {
  set.seed(5080)
  unique_properties <- sample(unique(data$property_group))
  stopifnot(length(unique_properties) >= 10)
  property_folds <- rep(1:10, length.out = length(unique_properties))
  property_folds[match(data$property_group, unique_properties)]
}

folds <- make_folds(development)
stopifnot(length(intersect(development$property_group, audit$property_group)) == 0)
validation_samples <- tibble(
  sample = c("Development: model comparison", "Audit: previously inspected", "All cleaned training", "Instructor test: no outcomes"),
  rows = c(nrow(development), nrow(audit), nrow(train), nrow(test)),
  property_groups = c(n_distinct(development$property_group), n_distinct(audit$property_group),
                      n_distinct(train$property_group), n_distinct(test$property_group)))
knitr::kable(validation_samples, caption = "Roles and sizes of the evaluation samples")
```

### Specify the candidate models

Each formula is written out as `f0`, `f1`, and so on, as in the notes. `I(x^2)` adds a squared term, factors add place or time categories, and `building_000sf:ring` adds the size-by-ring interaction. `log1p(lotsize_acre)` means `log(1 + lotsize_acre)`, which is defined at zero. We also compare cubic coordinate terms as an extension of the notes' squared-term approach.

```{r}
#| label: candidate-formulas
# Explicit formulas, following the f0/f1 pattern in Weeks 6 and 7.
# Missingness indicators retain the same fitting recipe as before.
f0 <- sale_price ~ building_000sf + building_age + lotsize_acre + num_bedrooms + num_full_baths +
    num_half_baths + num_fireplaces + garage_size + central_air + one_story + full_basement +
    finished_basement + brick_stone_ext + warmairfurnace

f1 <- sale_price ~ building_000sf + building_age + num_bedrooms + num_full_baths + num_half_baths +
    num_fireplaces + garage_size + central_air + one_story + full_basement + finished_basement +
    brick_stone_ext + warmairfurnace + log1p(lotsize_acre) + I(building_000sf^2) + I(building_age^2) +
    year_f + quarter_f + num_half_baths_missing + num_fireplaces_missing +
    garage_size_missing + full_basement_missing + warmairfurnace_missing

f2 <- sale_price ~ building_age + num_bedrooms + num_full_baths + num_half_baths + num_fireplaces +
    garage_size + central_air + one_story + full_basement + finished_basement + brick_stone_ext +
    warmairfurnace + log1p(lotsize_acre) + I(building_age^2) + year_f + quarter_f + 
    num_half_baths_missing + num_fireplaces_missing + garage_size_missing + full_basement_missing +
    warmairfurnace_missing + log(building_000sf)

f3 <- sale_price ~ building_000sf + building_age + num_bedrooms + num_full_baths + num_half_baths +
    num_fireplaces + garage_size + central_air + one_story + full_basement + finished_basement +
    brick_stone_ext + warmairfurnace + log1p(lotsize_acre) + I(building_000sf^2) + I(building_age^2) +
    year_f + quarter_f + num_half_baths_missing + num_fireplaces_missing +
```

### Define cross-validation and residual spatial diagnostics

The spatial diagnostic follows Week 7: `knearneigh(k = 5)` → `knn2nb()` → `nb2listw(style = "W")`. Duplicate coordinates use the notes' `use_kd_tree` check rather than artificial coordinate offsets. Moran's I values therefore differ from the earlier 8-neighbor symmetric definition. The same weights are used for every candidate in this run.

```{r}
#| label: validation-functions
# Week 7's prediction loop, with fitting-fold imputation added.
cv_predictions <- function(formula, data, fold_id) {
  stopifnot(nrow(data) == length(fold_id), !anyNA(fold_id))
  predictions <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(data))

  for (k in sort(unique(fold_id))) {
    validation_rows <- fold_id == k
    fitting <- prepare(data[!validation_rows, ], data[!validation_rows, ])
    validating <- prepare(data[validation_rows, ], data[!validation_rows, ])

    # Check factor coverage as in Week 6.
    category_vars <- c("tract_fe", "grid_fe", "ring", "year_f", "quarter_f")
    for (v in category_vars) {
      training_levels <- unique(as.character(fitting[[v]]))
      validation_levels <- unique(as.character(validating[[v]]))
      unseen_levels <- setdiff(validation_levels, training_levels)
      if (length(unseen_levels) > 0) {
        stop("A validation category is absent from the fitting rows.")
      }
    }

    fit <- lm(formula, data = fitting, na.action = na.fail)
    stopifnot(!anyNA(coef(fit)))
    predictions[validation_rows] <- predict(fit, newdata = validating)
  }

  stopifnot(all(is.finite(predictions)))
  predictions
}

make_weights <- function(data) {
  coords <- st_coordinates(data)
  house_knn <- knearneigh(coords, k = 5, longlat = FALSE,
                         use_kd_tree = anyDuplicated(coords) == 0)
  house_nb <- knn2nb(house_knn)
  nb2listw(house_nb, style = "W")
}
moran_i <- function(values, weights) {
  moran(values, weights, n = length(values), S0 = Szero(weights))$I
}
```

### Fit and compare the candidates

```{r}
#| label: part-2
weights <- make_weights(development)

# Evaluate the formula list as in Week 7.
cv_results <- lapply(models, function(f) {
  predictions <- cv_predictions(f, development, folds)
  errors <- development$sale_price - predictions
  list(pred = predictions, rmse = sqrt(mean(errors^2)))
})

model_log <- imap_dfr(cv_results, function(result, model_name) {
  tibble(
    model = model_name,
    cv_rmse = result$rmse,
    moran_i = moran_i(development$sale_price - result$pred, weights)
  )
}) %>%
  mutate(
    added = notes,
    notes = "Same grouped folds, development sample; pooled dollar RMSE"
  ) %>%
  select(model, added, cv_rmse, moran_i, notes)

# Add the zero-bound alternatives using the notes' add_row() pattern.
raw_names <- names(models)
for (model_name in raw_names) {
  bounded_name <- paste0(model_name, "_nonnegative")
  models[[bounded_name]] <- models[[model_name]]
  predictions <- if_else(cv_results[[model_name]]$pred < 0, 0, cv_results[[model_name]]$pred)
  errors <- development$sale_price - predictions
  cv_results[[bounded_name]] <- list(
    pred = predictions,
    rmse = sqrt(mean(errors^2))
  )

  model_log <- model_log %>%
    add_row(
      model = bounded_name,
      added = paste("Same formula as", model_name, "; constrain predicted values to >= $0"),
      cv_rmse = sqrt(mean(errors^2)),
      moran_i = moran_i(errors, weights),
      notes = "Domain constraint; all 12 alternatives evaluated on the same held-out predictions"
    )
}

knitr::kable(model_log %>% mutate(cv_rmse = money(cv_rmse), moran_i = round(moran_i, 3)),
             caption = "All tried specifications, in order: development-sample grouped 10-fold CV")
```

### Features and validation design

- House features: size, age, rooms and other supplied measurements. We also test squared terms, log lot area, year and quarter categories, and flags for missing values.
- Location features: distance from a fixed point in the Loop, rings at 3 and 8 miles, coordinate terms, Census tracts and 2-mile grid cells. Grid cells are not official neighborhoods. Each fitting sample decides which small area categories to combine; sale prices are not used for this decision.
- Interactions: the size–price relationship can differ by distance ring. Area fixed effects give each area its own starting price level, also called an intercept.

We use `r nrow(development)` sales to compare models and hold out `r nrow(audit)` for the audit. Every candidate uses the same 10 development folds. We round longitude and latitude to five decimal places to keep likely repeat-property records together. No coordinate group appears in both development and audit. Without parcel IDs, though, we cannot confirm that this catches every repeat sale. Nearby houses can still fall in different folds.

Each out-of-fold prediction comes from a model that did not fit that house's fold. We square all these errors, take their mean, and then take the square root to get RMSE in dollars. This is different from averaging ten separate fold RMSEs. For the spatial check, each house has five nearby houses as neighbors. Their weights add to one. We use the same locations and weights for all models, so the comparisons are fair.

Earlier versions of the 12 formulas gave some negative test predictions. We therefore also compare versions that replace negative predictions with zero. We use the same rule in CV, the audit sample and the test file. For a positive sale price, replacing a negative prediction with zero always reduces squared error. This is a rule about possible house values, not new information learned by the model. We had already looked at the audit sample before adding this rule, so the audit is not a completely independent check. We do not use audit scores to choose the winning formula.

The ACS income figures cover 2019–2023. We use them only to describe income-related error patterns, not to predict prices, because they were released after some of these sales. We use 2023 tract boundaries throughout. Our random grouped splits test predictions for other houses in the observed period; they do not test forecasting a later year.

Sources: [2023 ACS API](https://api.census.gov/data/2023/acs/acs5.html), [B19013 table metadata](https://api.census.gov/data/2023/acs/acs5/groups/B19013.html), [2023 Census cartographic tract boundaries](https://www2.census.gov/geo/tiger/GENZ2023/shp/). We do not use neighboring sale prices or treat current amenities as historical observations.

## Part 3: Final model

Show your final model, the model log, and baseline vs. final residual maps.

### Select the winner and evaluate it on the audit sample

```{r}
#| label: select-and-audit
best_name <- model_log$model[which.min(model_log$cv_rmse)]
f_final <- models[[best_name]]
# Audit sample: not used to rank formulas; see the procedural caveat below.
dev_prepared <- prepare(development, development)
audit_prepared <- prepare(audit, development)
baseline_fit <- lm(baseline, data = dev_prepared, na.action = na.fail)
selected_fit <- lm(f_final, data = dev_prepared, na.action = na.fail)
audit_baseline <- predict(baseline_fit, newdata = audit_prepared)
audit_pred <- predict(selected_fit, newdata = audit_prepared)
stopifnot(all(is.finite(audit_baseline)), all(is.finite(audit_pred)))
if (endsWith(best_name, "_nonnegative")) audit_pred <- if_else(audit_pred < 0, 0, audit_pred)
audit_scores <- tibble(model = c("Baseline", best_name),
  rmse = c(sqrt(mean((audit$sale_price - audit_baseline)^2)), sqrt(mean((audit$sale_price - audit_pred)^2))),
  mae = c(mean(abs(audit$sale_price - audit_baseline)), mean(abs(audit$sale_price - audit_pred))))
audit <- audit %>% mutate(baseline_pred = audit_baseline, baseline_ratio = baseline_pred / sale_price,
                          pred = audit_pred, residual = sale_price - pred,
                          abs_error = abs(residual), ratio = pred / sale_price)
```

**Answer: What helped most, and what disappointed you?**

```{r}
#| label: answer-model-evidence
# Compare matched specifications; each contrast states exactly what changed.
comparison_pairs <- tibble(
  from = c("M0_structure", "M1_curved_time", "M1_curved_time", "M3_downtown",
           "M1_curved_time", "M8_tract_effects", "M9_tract_size_ring"),
  to = c("M1_curved_time", "M2_log_size", "M3_downtown", "M4_distance_curve",
         "M8_tract_effects", "M9_tract_size_ring", "M11_grid_effects"),
  change = c("Combined curvature, timing, missingness and lot transformation",
             "Replace quadratic size with log size", "Add linear downtown distance",
             "Add squared downtown distance", "Add tract intercepts",
             "Add rings and size-by-ring interactions",
             "Replace tract intercepts with grid intercepts")
)
comparisons <- comparison_pairs %>%
  left_join(model_log %>% select(from = model, rmse_before = cv_rmse, i_before = moran_i), by = "from") %>%
  left_join(model_log %>% select(to = model, rmse_after = cv_rmse, i_after = moran_i), by = "to") %>%
  mutate(rmse_reduction = rmse_before - rmse_after,
         proportional_reduction = rmse_reduction / rmse_before)
knitr::kable(comparisons %>%
  select(change, rmse_before, rmse_after, proportional_reduction, i_before, i_after) %>%
  mutate(across(c(rmse_before, rmse_after), money),
         proportional_reduction = pct(proportional_reduction),
         across(c(i_before, i_after), ~ round(.x, 3))),
  caption = "Matched raw-model comparisons. Positive RMSE reduction means improvement; negative means deterioration.")
strongest <- comparisons %>% arrange(desc(rmse_reduction)) %>% slice_head(n = 1)
log_comparison <- comparisons %>% filter(to == "M2_log_size")
selected_description <- notes[match(sub("_nonnegative$", "", best_name), raw_names)]
```

We chose `r best_name` because it had the lowest development CV RMSE: `r money(best_row$cv_rmse)`. The baseline RMSE was `r money(baseline_row$cv_rmse)`, so the reduction was `r pct(1 - best_row$cv_rmse / baseline_row$cv_rmse)`. The model log describes this model as **`r selected_description`**. Its full formula is shown above. `r if (endsWith(best_name, "_nonnegative")) "We also replace negative predictions with zero." else "We use the predictions directly, without a zero bound."`

The largest improvement in the comparison table came from **`r strongest$change`**. RMSE fell from `r money(strongest$rmse_before)` to `r money(strongest$rmse_after)`, or `r pct(strongest$proportional_reduction)`. Some comparisons change several features together. For example, M1 adds more than squared terms, so we cannot say that squared terms alone caused its improvement.

Replacing quadratic size with log size changed RMSE from `r money(log_comparison$rmse_before)` to `r money(log_comparison$rmse_after)`: `r ifelse(log_comparison$rmse_reduction > 0, "an improvement", ifelse(log_comparison$rmse_reduction < 0, "a deterioration", "no change"))` of `r money(abs(log_comparison$rmse_reduction))`. Baseline-to-selected residual Moran's I changed from `r round(baseline_row$moran_i, 3)` to `r round(best_row$moran_i, 3)`. Positive Moran's I indicates clustering of similar errors; it does not identify the cause. RMSE and spatial clustering measure different weaknesses.

On the separate audit sample, RMSE was `r money(audit_scores$rmse[2])`, compared with `r money(audit_scores$rmse[1])` for the baseline. We had looked at this sample before finishing the prediction rule, so it is not a fully independent final test. This is the best model among the options we tried, not the best possible model.

We leave out the lot-size missing-value flag because it does not vary in the development sample. The model cannot learn an effect from a column that is always zero. We still fill missing lot size with the fitting-sample median. The other five missing-value flags stay in the models.

**4A.** Where does your final model fail worst? Is it guessing too high or too low there, and why do you think so?

**4B.** Assessors judge their work with the **ratio** of predicted value to sale price. A ratio above 1 means the home is over-valued and its owner over-taxed. Does your model's ratio differ by neighborhood income? Connect your answer to your Part 1 cleaning rules and to "The Tax Divide."

```{r}
#| label: error-diagnostics
# Retrospective income context is deliberately excluded from all model formulas.
cuts <- quantile(income$income[is.finite(income$income)], c(1/3, 2/3), names = FALSE)
audit <- audit %>% mutate(income_group = factor(case_when(
  is.na(income) ~ "Unknown", income <= cuts[1] ~ "Lower", income <= cuts[2] ~ "Middle", TRUE ~ "Higher"),
  levels = c("Lower", "Middle", "Higher", "Unknown")))

  n = n(), properties = n_distinct(property_group),

  baseline_median_ratio = median(baseline_ratio), median_ratio = median(ratio),
  change_in_distance_from_one = abs(median(ratio) - 1) - abs(median(baseline_ratio) - 1),
  aggregate_ratio = sum(pred) / sum(sale_price), share_overvalued = mean(ratio > 1),

  mutate(price_group = ntile(sale_price, 4)) %>% group_by(price_group) %>% summarize(

  n = n(), mae = mean(abs_error), mean_residual = mean(residual), .groups = "drop") %>%

stopifnot(nrow(geographic_errors) > 0)
worst <- audit %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% arrange(desc(abs_error)) %>%
  select(id, tract, sale_price, pred, residual, building_000sf, income_group) %>% slice_head(n = 10)
income_cuts <- cuts
audit_moran <- moran_i(audit$residual, make_weights(audit))
validation <- list(unmatched_tracts = sum(is.na(all_sales$tract)))
```

**4A.** Among tracts with at least 10 audit sales, tract `r geographic_errors$tract[1]` had the largest MAE: `r money(geographic_errors$mae[1])`. MAE is the average size of an error, ignoring its sign. This tract had `r geographic_errors$n[1]` audit sales. Its mean residual was `r money(geographic_errors$mean_residual[1])`, so predictions were `r ifelse(geographic_errors$mean_residual[1] > 0, "too low on average", ifelse(geographic_errors$mean_residual[1] < 0, "too high on average", "correct on average in this sample"))`. The map below shows its location. This ranking describes our audit sample; it does not prove which area has the worst errors across all homes.

The largest individual error was record `r worst$id[1]`. It sold for `r money(worst$sale_price[1])`, but the model predicted `r money(worst$pred[1])`. Missing information about condition, unusual luxury houses or incorrect area measurements could explain large errors. These are possible explanations, not proven causes. Audit Moran's I was `r round(audit_moran, 3)`. A positive value means similar errors tend to occur nearby, but the value alone is not a significance test. Predicting a later year or a completely new area could be harder than our current validation task.

### Week 8: Where do similar errors occur?

Global Moran's I gives one number for all houses. **Local Moran's I**, used in LISA, helps us find the places that need a closer look. We compare the baseline and final model on the same development houses, using the same five-neighbor weights. Each prediction was made without fitting that house's CV fold. This is an extra diagnostic, not a new predictor or a new model-selection rule.

We first subtract the mean error from each residual. This is called **centering**. High means above the mean error; low means below it. We then compare each house with its neighbors.

| Group | Meaning |
|---|---|
| High-High | The house and its neighbors have errors above the mean |
| Low-Low | The house and its neighbors have errors below the mean |
| High-Low | The house is above the mean, but its neighbors are below it |
| Low-High | The house is below the mean, but its neighbors are above it |
| Not flagged | The local test did not flag one of these four patterns |

High-High and Low-Low are local clusters. The other two groups are spatial outliers: houses that differ from their neighbors. **Low-Low does not automatically mean overprediction.** We must also check whether the actual residual is negative.

```{r}
#| label: local-error-groups
# Week 8: 499 permutations, the same weights, and a 0.01 threshold.
lisa_groups <- function(predictions, model_name) {
  errors <- development$sale_price - predictions
  centered <- errors - mean(errors)
  neighbor_error <- lag.listw(weights, centered)
  local_test <- localmoran_perm(errors, weights, nsim = 499,
                                alternative = "two.sided", iseed = 5080)
  p_value <- local_test[, "Pr(z != E(Ii)) Sim"]
  stopifnot(all(is.finite(p_value)))

  development %>% mutate(
    model = model_name,
    residual = errors,
    group = case_when(
      p_value < .01 & centered > 0 & neighbor_error > 0 ~ "High-High",
      p_value < .01 & centered < 0 & neighbor_error < 0 ~ "Low-Low",
      p_value < .01 & centered > 0 & neighbor_error < 0 ~ "High-Low",
      p_value < .01 & centered < 0 & neighbor_error > 0 ~ "Low-High",
      TRUE ~ "Not flagged"
    ),
    group = factor(group, levels = c("High-High", "Low-Low", "High-Low",
                                     "Low-High", "Not flagged"))
  )
}
lisa_results <- bind_rows(
  lisa_groups(cv_results[["M0_structure"]]$pred, "Baseline"),
  lisa_groups(cv_results[[best_name]]$pred, "Final")
)
lisa_summary <- lisa_results %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(model, group, .drop = FALSE) %>% summarize(
    houses = n(),
    mean_residual = if (n() > 0) mean(residual) else NA_real_,
    share_overpredicted = if (n() > 0) mean(residual < 0) else NA_real_,
    .groups = "drop"
  )
knitr::kable(lisa_summary %>% mutate(mean_residual = money(mean_residual),
  share_overpredicted = pct(share_overpredicted)),
  caption = "Local groups on development CV predictions. The last column checks actual residual signs.")
```

```{r}
#| label: local-error-map
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Baseline and final local error groups on the same houses. Flags use unadjusted permutation p-values below 0.01. Grey does not mean the prediction is accurate."
ggplot(lisa_results %>% arrange(group != "Not flagged")) +
  geom_sf(aes(color = group), size = .35, alpha = .7) +
  facet_wrap(~model) + coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("High-High" = "#B2182B", "Low-Low" = "#2166AC",
    "High-Low" = "#E69F00", "Low-High" = "#009E73", "Not flagged" = "grey80"),
    drop = FALSE, name = "Local error group") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

The baseline has `r sum(lisa_results$model == "Baseline" & lisa_results$group == "Low-Low")` Low-Low flags; the final model has `r sum(lisa_results$model == "Final" & lisa_results$group == "Low-Low")`. High-High flags change from `r sum(lisa_results$model == "Baseline" & lisa_results$group == "High-High")` to `r sum(lisa_results$model == "Final" & lisa_results$group == "High-High")`. These counts show local patterns, not how large the dollar errors are. As Week 8 explains, lower RMSE does not always mean fewer local clusters.

The test uses 499 randomized comparisons for each house and a p-value threshold of 0.01. We use a two-sided test so both clusters and spatial outliers can be flagged. We do not adjust the p-values for the large number of tests. Some flags may therefore occur by chance. These maps help us choose places to investigate; they do not prove a cause. Not flagged also does not mean correct.

### Local error patterns by area income

This next table uses the **final model's development CV errors**. The valuation-ratio tables above use the separate **audit sample**. Their sample sizes differ, so their percentages answer different questions. We use the same income cutoffs in both tables.

```{r}
#| label: local-errors-by-income
lisa_income <- lisa_results %>% filter(model == "Final") %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>% mutate(income_group = factor(case_when(
    is.na(income) ~ "Unknown", income <= cuts[1] ~ "Lower",
    income <= cuts[2] ~ "Middle", TRUE ~ "Higher"),
    levels = c("Lower", "Middle", "Higher", "Unknown"))) %>%
  group_by(income_group) %>% summarize(
    houses = n(),
    low_low = sum(group == "Low-Low"),
    low_low_share = mean(group == "Low-Low"),
    low_low_and_overpredicted = sum(group == "Low-Low" & residual < 0),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
knitr::kable(lisa_income %>% mutate(low_low_share = pct(low_low_share)),
  caption = "Local flags by tract income. The final column counts Low-Low houses whose prices were actually overpredicted.")
```

The Low-Low share is `r pct(lisa_income$low_low_share[lisa_income$income_group == "Lower"])` in lower-income areas and `r pct(lisa_income$low_low_share[lisa_income$income_group == "Higher"])` in higher-income areas. These are patterns in this sample, not a test of the difference between income groups. Area income does not tell us an individual owner's income.

A cluster gives us a question to investigate. For example, condition, vacancy or access to services might matter. We would need suitable data from the allowed period before adding a new feature. We would then compare models using the same CV folds. We do not use neighboring sale prices or the instructor's hidden test prices to build a feature.
```{r}
#| label: income-answer-evidence
lower_ratio <- fairness$median_ratio[fairness$income_group == "Lower"]
higher_ratio <- fairness$median_ratio[fairness$income_group == "Higher"]
stopifnot(length(lower_ratio) == 1, length(higher_ratio) == 1,
          is.finite(lower_ratio), is.finite(higher_ratio))
ratio_interpretation <- function(x) {
  if (x > 1) paste(pct(x - 1), "overprediction")
  else if (x < 1) paste(pct(1 - x), "underprediction")
  else "no median proportional error"
}
```
**4B.** We divide Cook County tracts into three income groups, using cutoffs of `r money(income_cuts[1])` and `r money(income_cuts[2])`. These groups contain roughly equal numbers of tracts, not equal numbers of houses or residents. The lower-income group's median ratio was `r round(lower_ratio, 3)`, compared with `r round(higher_ratio, 3)` for the higher-income group. The difference was `r round(abs(lower_ratio - higher_ratio), 3)` ratio units, with the lower-income group's ratio `r ifelse(lower_ratio > higher_ratio, "higher", ifelse(lower_ratio < higher_ratio, "lower", "the same"))`.

Compared with 1, these medians show `r ratio_interpretation(lower_ratio)` in the lower-income group and `r ratio_interpretation(higher_ratio)` in the higher-income group. A higher ratio does not always mean overprediction: both ratios could be below 1. These results describe the sample; we have not tested whether the group difference is statistically significant.

The baseline and final ratios use the same audit sales. In the table, a negative change in distance from 1 means that the group's median ratio improved. This does not mean every house improved. The aggregate ratio is the sum of predictions divided by the sum of sale prices. It gives more weight to expensive houses than the median individual ratio does.

We also check the cheapest quarter of audit sales. Its median ratio was `r round(price_fairness$median_ratio[1], 3)`, showing `r ratio_interpretation(price_fairness$median_ratio[1])`. Cheap houses and low-income areas are not the same group. Lower dollar RMSE does not guarantee small percentage errors for cheap houses. Also, models often predict extreme prices closer to the middle. Grouping by actual price can show this pattern even without discrimination.

We kept cheap sales because a low price alone does not show that a sale is wrong. We removed multi-parcel sales because one price may cover several properties. Our audit therefore does not show how well the model predicts those bundled test transactions. Like the *Tax Divide* discussion, we ask whether cheap homes receive larger errors relative to their prices. These are prediction checks, not actual tax calculations or proof that income causes the errors. [The Tax Divide investigation](https://apps.chicagotribune.com/news/watchdog/cook-county-property-tax-divide/).

An area's income is not the same as an owner's income. ACS income estimates also have sampling error. Across all input rows, `r validation$unmatched_tracts` houses had no tract match. We kept those houses and did not give them income from a nearby tract.

```{r}
#| label: predict-test

preds <- tibble(id = test$id, pred = predict(m_final, newdata = final_test))
if (endsWith(best_name, "_nonnegative")) preds$pred <- if_else(preds$pred < 0, 0, preds$pred)
stopifnot(nrow(preds) == nrow(test), !anyDuplicated(preds$id),
          identical(preds$id, test$id), identical(preds$id, raw_test$id), all(is.finite(preds$pred)), all(preds$pred >= 0))
knitr::kable(head(preds), caption = "First six exported predictions")
knitr::kable(tibble(test_rows = nrow(test), exported_rows = nrow(preds),

write_csv(model_log, file.path(report_dir, "model_log.csv"))
write_csv(preds, file.path(report_dir, "team_XX_predictions.csv"))
review_predictions <- test %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(id, building_000sf, building_age, tract, is_multisale) %>%

write_csv(review_predictions, file.path(report_dir, "predictions_needing_review.csv"))
knitr::kable(review_predictions, caption = "Zero-valued test predictions requiring review; none removed from the export")
```

Our model-selection grouped 10-fold CV RMSE is `r money(best_row$cv_rmse)`. The separate audit RMSE is `r money(audit_scores$rmse[2])`. We will only know the instructor's test RMSE after scoring.

We save the predictions to `reports/assignment5_modified/team_XX_predictions.csv`, with all `r nrow(preds)` test IDs in their original order. We still need to replace `XX` with our team number before uploading. The zero bound affects `r sum(preds$pred == 0)` predictions. Those houses need review: zero is a sign that the model has failed for those records, not a believable house value. We do not cap high predictions or add a positive price floor.

## Part 6: Reflection (about 300 words, as a team)

1. **Read one coefficient twice:** once as β̂, once for what it does to ŷ.
2. **Would you hand this model to the Assessor?** What would you warn them about?

We started with house features and then tested location. Similar houses can have different prices in different parts of Chicago. Our selected model is `r best_name`. Its features help prediction, but they do not prove what changing a house would cause.

The `central_air` coefficient is `r money(unname(coef(m_final)["central_air"]))`. If 0 means no central air and 1 means central air, beta-hat is the estimated price difference when the other inputs stay the same. For y-hat, changing 0 to 1 adds this amount to the raw prediction. A $300,000 prediction becomes `r money(300000 + unname(coef(m_final)["central_air"]))`. The zero bound can change this difference near zero. We still need to confirm the source coding. This coefficient does not tell us the return from installing air conditioning, because condition and renovations may also differ.

We would not use this model for real assessments yet. The cheapest quarter of audit sales has a median ratio of `r round(price_fairness$median_ratio[1], 3)`, or `r ratio_interpretation(price_fairness$median_ratio[1])`. Week 8 adds another check: LISA shows where similar errors occur. Low-Low means below the mean error, so we also check the actual error signs. Neither a good RMSE nor a local flag proves that an assessment is fair.

Week 8 also asks how people use predictions. Even an accurate model needs clear rules, human review and a way for owners to question errors. We use public data and supplied house records; we do not use competitors' private pricing data.

We kept extreme prices unless we had evidence to remove them, but excluded bundled transactions. The audit was viewed during development, so it is not a fully independent test. Before real use, we would check later years, new areas and missing property details. The zero predictions need review because they are model failures, not believable house values.
